overview.text: The OCA identifies the Inexhaustible Chalice as an Orans image and links its veneration with Serpukhov and a retired soldier’s recovery from destructive drinking. Its account differentiates the original, whose later whereabouts are unknown, from subsequent copies.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph; paragraphs on 1919 and later copies

blocks.text: The Mother of God raises her hands in prayer. Before her, the Christ Child stands in a chalice. The source explicitly identifies this as the Communion chalice, rather than interpreting the vessel as an ordinary drinking cup.

blocks.text: The church narrative places the soldier in Tula Province in 1878. Repeated dreams direct him to a monastery at Serpukhov. The nuns initially do not recognize the requested icon, then find its name inscribed on the reverse. He recognizes Saint Barlaam of Serpukhov as the elder from his dream. The OCA recounts the soldier’s deliverance, the closure of the monastery in 1919, and the revival of veneration through copies made in 1993 and 1995.

blocks.text: The published meaning emphasizes consolation, mercy, and repentance. The entry says the precise day of the icon’s revelation is unknown; it records the church-wide celebration on May 5 established in 1997 in connection with Saint Barlaam’s commemoration.
